trap.wrong: "Alert when CPU goes above 80% or a pod restarts."
trap.why: Cause-based thresholds page on things users never feel and train on-call to ignore pages.
trap.probe: Symptom-based paging tied to SLOs, burn rates, a runbook per alert, deleting noise.
trap.say: "Page only on fast SLO burn for user journeys, ticket on causes, link every alert to a runbook, and delete alerts nobody acts on."

thesis: Page a human only for symptoms users feel, measured against SLOs, and only when someone needs to act now. Causes such as high CPU or a full disk become tickets or dashboard signals unless they're about to cause user pain. Every page has an owner and a runbook, and alerts that never lead to action get deleted.
pitch: Noise comes from paging on causes: CPU above 80%, a pod restart, a queue above a number. Most of those don't hurt users, and the ones that do will show up as symptoms. So I'd page on symptoms tied to SLOs: error rate and latency for key user journeys, ideally as error-budget burn rate, which naturally ignores short blips and catches slow burns. Cause-based alerts that predict imminent pain, like a disk filling within four hours or a certificate expiring in seven days, are fine as tickets or business-hours alerts. Every alert must answer: who owns it, what does the responder do, and why now? Each links to a runbook. Then hygiene: track alert volume per on-call shift and the fraction that led to action; review regularly; delete or downgrade alerts that are routinely acknowledged and ignored; group and deduplicate related alerts so one incident means one page.

points.d: User-facing error rates, latency and availability for key journeys. These capture all causes, including ones you didn't predict.
Multi-window burn-rate alerts page when the error budget is being consumed fast and resolve quickly when it stops. They ignore brief blips.
Capacity trends, single-instance failures, certificate expiry and disk growth become tickets or daytime notifications unless user impact is imminent.
Each alert has an owning team, a severity, and a runbook link. If there's nothing to do, it shouldn't page.
One incident should produce one page, with related alerts grouped under it. Alert storms bury the signal.
Pages per shift, percent actionable, time to acknowledge, and repeat offenders. Review in on-call handoffs.
Alerts that were ignored repeatedly are removed or downgraded. Keeping them trains people to ignore pages.

decision: Pages: SLO burn-rate and hard user-facing outages only. Tickets: predictive cause-based signals. Dashboards: everything else. Revisit alert rules after every incident and every few months.
numbers: On-call health target from the Google SRE book: at most about two incidents per 12-hour shift, so each gets proper attention.
Fast-burn example: page when burning 14.4x budget over both 1 hour and 5 minutes; slow-burn ticket at 1x over 3 days.
pitfalls: Static thresholds on CPU or memory that page at night with no user impact.
Alerts without runbooks, so responders improvise.
Duplicate alerts from every layer for the same outage.
Never deleting alerts, so the on-call rotation learns to ignore the pager.

followups.q: How do you catch problems that aren't covered by SLOs?
followups.a: Add synthetic checks for important paths, and review incidents to see whether a missing SLI should be added.
Alert on symptoms too: job didn't complete by its deadline, or output freshness exceeded its target.

followups.q: How do you reduce a noisy rotation quickly?
followups.a: Pull a month of pages, classify actionable vs not, delete or downgrade the non-actionable ones, and fix the top recurring causes.

example: A team receiving 40 pages a week replaced 60 threshold alerts with burn-rate alerts on four SLOs plus ticketed capacity warnings. Pages dropped to about four a week, and every one was a real customer-facing problem.
